A magistrate judge ordered Donald Trump to sit for questioning in his defamation case against the BBC by December 11, warning that the complaint could be dismissed if he does not comply. Trump is seeking $10 billion in damages from the BBC over the documentary's portrayal of his remarks.1

Trump called off an earlier deposition scheduled for October 16, pointing to a matter of national importance.1

The defamation action was formally filed on December 15 against the broadcaster.3

U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett has directed Donald Trump to provide a deposition in his $10 billion defamation case against the BBC by December 11.1 The order gives a final date for Trump’s questioning and says that failure to meet it could result in dismissal of his complaint.1 The case is Trump’s lawsuit against the broadcaster, and the stated amount at issue is $10 billion.1 The order addresses a deposition that had not happened, despite a previous date being set and the discovery period nearing its end.12 The immediate change is therefore a court-imposed deadline, paired with a stated consequence if Trump does not appear.1

Trump had earlier been due to give testimony on October 16, but he called off that appearance.1 He explained the cancellation by referring to what he described as a matter of national importance.1 BBC lawyer Charles Tobin told the court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia on the day the deposition was cancelled.1 The available account thus sets out both Trump’s stated reason for cancelling and Tobin’s description of his activity that day.1 Those details explain why the October date did not resolve the question of when the plaintiff would be deposed; Lett’s later order supplied a new deadline.1

The timing became a point of dispute because the discovery period had only two months remaining while Trump still had not given a deposition.2 Tobin made that observation to the judge, describing the plaintiff’s deposition as still outstanding at that stage.2 Trump’s lawyers, by contrast, asked for the testimony to be scheduled during a window from January 11 through January 22, 2025.3 That requested window came after the December 11 date in Lett’s order, making the parties’ positions on timing materially different.13 The judge’s warning ties compliance to the survival of the complaint, rather than merely setting another proposed date for testimony.13

The case began with a filing on December 15 that challenged the BBC documentary’s depiction of Trump.3 The complaint characterized that portrayal as false and defamatory, and also alleged that it was deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious.3 Those terms state the allegations made in the lawsuit; they do not establish that the BBC’s depiction was legally defamatory.13 The dispute includes an acknowledged edit in which filmmakers combined separate portions of Trump’s remarks from January 6.1 That editing decision is part of the account surrounding the complaint, while the BBC continues to deny that Trump has a valid basis for his defamation claim.13

The BBC’s response to the edited clip included an apology, and the broadcaster’s head and leading news executive resigned.1 The resignations and apology followed the BBC’s acknowledgment that the film combined different segments of Trump’s January 6 remarks.1 The apology did not amount to the BBC accepting that the lawsuit had a legal foundation, since the broadcaster denied that Trump had grounds for the claim.1 The record therefore distinguishes the BBC’s acknowledgment and institutional response from its position on the legal allegation.1 The deposition order concerns Trump’s role as the plaintiff, while the editing, apology, and resignations describe the broadcaster’s conduct and response.1

The BBC has also accused Trump’s legal team of slowing the exchange of evidence during discovery.3 In a filing, the broadcaster said the team returned documents that the BBC had already provided.3 The BBC further complained that Trump’s lawyers relied on web pages that were already publicly accessible.3 These are allegations made by the BBC about the other side’s handling of discovery, not findings stated by the judge.3 They sit alongside Tobin’s account that Trump had not been deposed with two months left in the evidence-gathering period.23

The question of who is affected by the order is direct: it requires Trump, as the plaintiff, to give the deposition by the date set by the court.12 The consequence specified is possible dismissal of his complaint if he fails to comply, rather than a stated change to the BBC’s position or its apology.1 The timing can be understood by comparing the cancelled October 16 appointment, the December 11 court deadline, and the later January 11 to January 22, 2025 window requested by Trump’s lawyers.13 The accounts do not describe those dates as equivalent: October 16 was the cancelled appointment, December 11 is the ordered deadline, and the January dates were the lawyers’ proposed range.13 The two-month discovery reference supplies a separate measure of urgency, describing how much time remained when Tobin raised the missing deposition.2

The wider concern raised around the case is about the use of litigation and legal threats in disputes over media coverage.1 Press-freedom advocates have expressed alarm about what they describe as a pattern in which Trump’s lawsuits can be used to influence coverage.1 That concern is distinct from the specific legal question in this suit, which the BBC disputes despite acknowledging the edit and apologizing for the clip.1 The available facts do not resolve the merits of Trump’s defamation claim; they establish the allegation, the BBC’s denial, and the judge’s order for testimony.13 For now, the procedural issue is whether Trump will meet the December 11 deadline after the earlier deposition was cancelled and the requested January scheduling window was rejected by the order.13

Trump’s on Marylanders’ minds, if not their ballots, as early voting begins

The Republican president isn’t on the ballot as Marylanders are picking their next governor, all eight members of the U.S. House of Representatives, the entire Maryland General Assembly, along with scores of local races. But that didn’t stop voters from talking about Donald Trump and national issues.

Actual Article Body:
Maryland’s in-person, early voting began across the state Thursday — and a politician who isn’t on the ballot motivated many to head to the polls.

Marylanders are voting whether to reelect Gov. Wes Moore and are picking all eight members of the U.S. House of Representatives, the entire Maryland General Assembly and weighing in on scores of local races.

But that didn’t stop voters from talking about Republican President Donald Trump and national issues.

Cheryl Davidow, 74, said she was voting at the Pip Moyer Recreation Center in Annapolis for anyone with a “D” next to their name — an expression of opposition to the way Republicans are handling the federal government, she said.

Davidow wore a knit hat with a blue wave on it that a friend made for her. Among the stitches were dots in Morse code with a flippant message for Trump.

“I’m just so fed up. I’m just so fed up,” she said.

Maryland’s polling stations opened on time, and as of 1 p.m., more than 40,000 voters had cast their ballots at early voting places, according to Election Administrator Jared DeMarinis.

Early voting continues daily through Oct. 29, and voters can cast ballots at any voting center in their county. Election Day is Nov. 3.

Mail balloting continues. By Wednesday night, 242,744 Marylanders had returned their ballots. Those can be mailed in or handed over at in-person voting sites or in drop boxes.

Voters across the state told The Banner they were concerned about affordability, immigration and funding for important programs.

Some blamed Trump and Republicans for their problems. Others emphasized the importance of voting in general, given that generations of Americans fought hard to gain and maintain the right to vote.

Briana Smith, 31, voted at the Randallstown Community Center in Baltimore County because, she said, “there are so many things happening with the Trump administration.”

“I feel like that is really affecting me here in Baltimore,” she added.

Smith said she is concerned about women’s rights, policing and immigration. Seeing footage of immigration agents roaming in Maryland is upsetting and unacceptable, she said.

She also talked about affordability, from funding cuts to disability services at her employer to the general cost of living.

“It feels really hard to live and to start a life in a family, and to also be a part of my community,” Smith said. “It feels hard having to work an excessive amount of hours just to live or an excessive amount of jobs.”

Not all voters were upset with Trump. In Severna Park, Republican Joanne Heath, 72, said she voted with her party to continue Trump’s agenda, even though he’s not on the ballot.

“I want America to be safe and free for our granddaughter,” Heath said after voting at the Earleigh Heights Volunteer Fire Station.

Maurice Wood, 74, who also voted in Randallstown, said he’s concerned about the economy and “things in Washington,” where he said he feels elected officials only care about “the rich folk and the dollar.”

In Baltimore, Bolton Hill resident Robert Currie cast his ballot at the University of Maryland, Baltimore’s Community Engagement Center.

“I believe the country has gone in the wrong direction over the last two years, and there’s a need for us to stand up and represent the humanity, the moral character, the high standards that America stands for,” said Currie, 67.

“It’s the government at the federal level that makes us look bad worldwide,” he added. “It’s not the citizens, and we can do better.”

Charisse Lue, 40, who lives in Baltimore’s Franklin Square neighborhood, said removing the Republican Party from power was her main motivation for voting this election.

“I think we’re at a critical time,” she said, “economically, socially, what direction of the country we go into.”

“I’m just hoping that these Democrats that we’re voting for will actually fight for our basic human rights, our civil rights to vote,” she said.

In Montgomery County, a group of about 30 voters walked together to a polling site in downtown Rockville, part of a rally to boost turnout.

One member of the group, Thea Miles, 84, of Rockville, said income inequality was a high priority when she cast her ballot. She said she hopes “wealth gets a little bit shared by everybody, not just the top.”

Voting is “sacred,” she added, because “a lot of people can’t in this world.”

As Maureen Kelly voted at the Bain 50+ Community Center in Columbia, she acknowledged: “I have a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome. I would love to see that man gone.”

“But,” she added with a shrug, “he’s not on the ballot.”

Banner reporters Olivia Bensimon, Antonio Planas, Lillian Reed, John-John Williams IV and Brenda Wintrode contributed to this article.

President Donald Trump’s affinity for his pal Vladimir Putin has now torpedoed new congressionally mandated sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine. How low will Trump stoop to aid Putin?...

President Donald Trump's affinity for his pal Vladimir Putin has now torpedoed new congressionally mandated sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine. How low will Trump stoop to aid Putin?

The trade restrictions that Trump lifted were named after Sen. Lindsey Graham, which passed with huge bipartisan support after Graham suddenly died this summer. But Trump used his authority to undermine the sanctions, ostensibly claiming to keep peace talks going. It's clear that this isn't about negotiation so much as helping his bud Putin secure a victory over Kyiv.

Indeed, Trump is pushing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal that seems a lot like outright capitulation, right after Starlink's military grade Starshield has intermittently gone down in Ukraine in recent days, leaving it more vulnerable for attack as U.S. intelligence allegedly curtailed information-sharing. Trump and his erstwhile ally Elon Musk have pointed the finger at each other for who's responsible, and frankly either or both could be lying.

And, of course, there is evidence that Russia is again trying to meddle in the U.S. midterm elections.

None of this is a surprise. Trump has never, ever understood or really cared about the realities for Ukraine in this conflict. He demonstrated that clearly enough even before this full-scale invasion even started, when he dangled cutting off U.S. military assistance to Kyiv as a threat to try to force Zelenskyy to investigate the family of Trump's political rival, Joe Biden, after Putin had already annexed the Crimea region. That was the "perfect phone call" for which he was impeached over.

Not much has changed and fast forward seven years and Trump is not only more out of control than ever, but he has completely subsumed the rest of the GOP into his fanatical movement, and is now undermining their goal of international security.

No amount of time atop the highest echelon of executive power has been able to convey to Trump the true stakes of his position and international diplomacy, nor to shake him out of seeing everything through the filter of the New York real estate world.

Everything to him is a deal, a deal in which he has to get his and the particulars are secondary. It is the guiding principle of all of his domestic and foreign policy goals, from the tariff obsession — which stems from a sophomoric understanding of international trade in which the U.S. must "win" by having a positive trade balance with every country in the world — to FEMA's disaster relief work to the Russia invasion.

He does not and cannot grasp the long-term consequences of a Russian victory in Ukraine, ranging from the sheer humanitarian disaster that would unfold on the ground to the threat to the rest of Europe, full of our own putative allies, and eventually to the U.S. itself.

The only thing Trump sees is that Putin is a "strong" leader — so because he terrorizes his domestic population, crushes political opposition, and sends many men to die in the name of his imperial ambitions — and that he could buy some of its gas to ease the self-inflicted political crisis of high prices at home, Ukraine, its people, and our allies be damned.

“I believe the country has gone in the wrong direction over the last two years, and there’s a need for us to stand up and represent the humanity, the moral character, the high standards that America stands for,” said Currie, 67.

“It’s the government at the federal level that makes us look bad worldwide,” he added. “It’s not the citizens, and we can do better.”

Charisse Lue, 40, who lives in Baltimore’s Franklin Square neighborhood, said removing the Republican Party from power was her main motivation for voting this election.

“I think we’re at a critical time,” she said, “economically, socially, what direction of the country we go into.”

“I’m just hoping that these Democrats that we’re voting for will actually fight for our basic human rights, our civil rights to vote,” she said.

In Montgomery County, a group of about 30 voters walked together to a polling site in downtown Rockville, part of a rally to boost turnout.

One member of the group, Thea Miles, 84, of Rockville, said income inequality was a high priority when she cast her ballot. She said she hopes “wealth gets a little bit shared by everybody, not just the top.”

Voting is “sacred,” she added, because “a lot of people can’t in this world.”

As Maureen Kelly voted at the Bain 50+ Community Center in Columbia, she acknowledged: “I have a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome. I would love to see that man gone.”

“But,” she added with a shrug, “he’s not on the ballot.”

Banner reporters Olivia Bensimon, Antonio Planas, Lillian Reed, John-John Williams IV and Brenda Wintrode contributed to this article.

President Donald Trump's affinity for his pal Vladimir Putin has now torpedoed new congressionally mandated sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine. How low will Trump stoop to aid Putin?

The trade restrictions that Trump lifted were named after Sen. Lindsey Graham, which passed with huge bipartisan support after Graham suddenly died this summer. But Trump used his authority to undermine the sanctions, ostensibly claiming to keep peace talks going. It's clear that this isn't about negotiation so much as helping his bud Putin secure a victory over Kyiv.

Indeed, Trump is pushing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal that seems a lot like outright capitulation, right after Starlink's military grade Starshield has intermittently gone down in Ukraine in recent days, leaving it more vulnerable for attack as U.S. intelligence allegedly curtailed information-sharing. Trump and his erstwhile ally Elon Musk have pointed the finger at each other for who's responsible, and frankly either or both could be lying.

And, of course, there is evidence that Russia is again trying to meddle in the U.S. midterm elections.

None of this is a surprise. Trump has never, ever understood or really cared about the realities for Ukraine in this conflict. He demonstrated that clearly enough even before this full-scale invasion even started, when he dangled cutting off U.S. military assistance to Kyiv as a threat to try to force Zelenskyy to investigate the family of Trump's political rival, Joe Biden, after Putin had already annexed the Crimea region. That was the "perfect phone call" for which he was impeached over.

Not much has changed and fast forward seven years and Trump is not only more out of control than ever, but he has completely subsumed the rest of the GOP into his fanatical movement, and is now undermining their goal of international security.

No amount of time atop the highest echelon of executive power has been able to convey to Trump the true stakes of his position and international diplomacy, nor to shake him out of seeing everything through the filter of the New York real estate world.

Everything to him is a deal, a deal in which he has to get his and the particulars are secondary. It is the guiding principle of all of his domestic and foreign policy goals, from the tariff obsession — which stems from a sophomoric understanding of international trade in which the U.S. must "win" by having a positive trade balance with every country in the world — to FEMA's disaster relief work to the Russia invasion.

He does not and cannot grasp the long-term consequences of a Russian victory in Ukraine, ranging from the sheer humanitarian disaster that would unfold on the ground to the threat to the rest of Europe, full of our own putative allies, and eventually to the U.S. itself.

The only thing Trump sees is that Putin is a "strong" leader — so because he terrorizes his domestic population, crushes political opposition, and sends many men to die in the name of his imperial ambitions — and that he could buy some of its gas to ease the self-inflicted political crisis of high prices at home, Ukraine, its people, and our allies be damned.
